newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gold mines seen reviewing hedge policies.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gold mines seen reviewing hedge policies.

text.p: Eyeing a weak bullion price and wary of a steadier rand, South African gold producers are caught between a rock and a hard place and are likely to review their hedging policies, analysts said.
"My feeling is that they are acutely aware that if the rand stabilises and if the gold price weakens they have a problem," gold hedging specialist Jessica Cross told Reuters.

With the recent security of a strong rand gold price fading, the country's gold mines could consider selling production forward in order to lock in a more attractive gold price for the future -- risking increased pressure on the bullion price.

"I suspect they are going to look at any way to protect their balance. Whether that means the existing hedges might be more actively managed, or there might be some topping up or even new entrants," Cross said.
Worries have surfaced that the bullion price will come under further pressure from increased supply if South African gold mines pour more gold into the market via forward sales.
But analysts said although this would be a negative factor, its damage would be limited by the magnitude of other factors in the market, including worry over central bank bullion sales.
"In the bigger scheme of things, I do not believe that further producer hedging out of South Africa is going to have a major influence on the gold price," Cross said.
"There have been so many other things going on in the international gold market that producer hedging has been somewhat sidelined."
The rand lost 29 percent of its value against the dollar in 1996 and gold mines grew fat on the robust rand gold price -- some respite from years of declining output.
But their moment in the sun appears to be over.
The rand looks steadier, bid at 4.6490 on the dollar on Tuesday afternoon, while bullion was imprisoned in a tight range and last stumbled just above $353 an ounce.

Having mostly shunned hedging, except for project-specific reasons, local gold mines are now likely to start experimenting -- aware of the benefits of well-managed policies and anxious about the soft bullion-steady rand situation, analysts said.

"I wouldn't be surprised if you saw a combination of hedging policies. They're starting to fine-tune their hedging, they're gaining a lot of experience in hedging," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Certain South African mining houses have shrugged off reviewing hedging policies because of the bullion-rand issue.

Gencor Ltd managing director Tom Dale said on Monday the weaker bullion price and expectations that the rand might stabilise in 1997 was unlikely to force the group to review its gold hedging strategy.

"I wouldn't think so. We're not natural hedgers like Anglo American. The Beatrix hedge was to protect a specific capital project," he told Reuters. He was referring to a long-term 90-tonne deal in 1995 to fund expansion of the No 3 shaft at Beatrix Mines Ltd.
Asked about Gold Fields anti-hedging policy, chief executive of gold operations Alan Munro said:

"It is true we don't have a forward position. Hindsight suggests it might have been a good thing to have locked in a better price. We benefit from not making forward sales when the price is increasing, it's going to do that one of these days."
Analysts say that hedging is a subjective tool, but its successes cannot be ignored.
Commenting on Gold Fields' non-hedging policy, Cross said:
"I am sure they must be watching closely developments in risk management...I think eventually something has to happen. You can't rest on your laurels, even if you consider yourself low cost."
